summary:
Stand on the **top-right** cell. If it's bigger than the target, its whole column (everything below it is even
bigger) can't contain the target: step left. If it's smaller, its whole row (everything to its left is
smaller) is out: step down. Each step removes a row or a column, so the search takes at most m + n steps.

question.md:
Every row is sorted left to right and every column top to bottom. Return true if `target` is in the grid.

- **Rows don't continue each other:** a row can start below the previous row's end, so the grid is *not* one
  long sorted list. (That's the difference from **Seat Map Lookup**.)
- **Duplicates** are allowed (non-decreasing).
- **Size:** up to 1000 × 1000 = 10⁶ cells.

think.caption: Top-right corner: the largest in its row, the smallest in its column.

think.md:
The top-left corner is useless as a start: both moves (right, down) increase the value. But the **top-right**
corner sits at a crossroads: moving left decreases, moving down increases. So one comparison decides a
direction:

- corner > target: the target can't be in this column (the rest of it is even larger): move left;
- corner < target: the target can't be in this row (the rest of it is even smaller): move down.

Each step eliminates a full row or column, so after at most m + n steps you either find the target or fall off
the grid. (The bottom-left corner works the same way, mirrored.)

approaches.title: Check every cell

idea.md: Compare every cell with the target.

build: Loop over all cells; return true on a match.

approaches.title: Binary-search each row

idea.md: Every row is sorted, so binary-search each row for the target.

build: For each row, run a lower-bound search for the target.
Return true if any row has it.

lines.text: Standard binary search within the sorted row.

complexity.md: **Time O(m log n):** about 10⁴ steps for 1000 × 1000. **Space O(1).**

steps.text: Row 2: binary search → found at column 1.

walk.title: Each row is sorted: binary-search every row.

limits.md: Uses the row order but not the column order. Using both lets each comparison discard a whole row or column.

approaches.title: Staircase walk from the top-right

idea.md: Start at (0, n − 1). Equal → true. Bigger than target → move left (drop the column). Smaller → move down (drop the row). Off the grid → false.

build: Return false when you leave the grid.

lines.text: The top-right corner: smallest of its column, largest of its row.
Too big: everything below in this column is at least as big, so the column is ruled out.
Too small: everything to the left in this row is at most as big, so the row is ruled out.
Every row or column was ruled out.

complexity.md: **Time O(m + n):** at most 2000 steps for 1000 × 1000. **Space O(1).**

steps.text: (0, 3) = 14 > 10: everything below it in column 3 is even bigger, so drop the column.
(0, 2) = 9 < 10: everything left of it in row 0 is even smaller, so drop the row.
(1, 2) = 11 > 10: everything below it in column 2 is even bigger, so drop the column.
(1, 1) = 7 < 10: everything left of it in row 1 is even smaller, so drop the row.

walk.title: Start at the top-right corner. Each comparison removes a whole row or a whole column.

takeaways.md:
- In a grid sorted by rows **and** columns, start at a corner where one direction increases and the other
  decreases (top-right or bottom-left). Each comparison discards a row or a column: O(m + n).
- If rows also continue each other, the grid is one sorted list and plain binary search gives O(log(m·n)).
